title: NY Surrogate's Court Guide (November 2026)
summary: Learn how NY Surrogate's Court works, including roles, fees, and forms executors should know in November 2026.
body_markdown:
During estate settlement in New York, Surrogate's Court validates wills and appoints the executor or administrator who has legal authority to act for the estate. That authority comes from court-issued papers, not from being named in a will or filing a petition. This guide explains key points for families and executors to be aware of, including: how the court is organized by county, the types of proceedings, who has authority to act, filing fees, forms, how to look up a case, and more.


**Key Takeaways**


- NY Surrogate's Court validates wills and appoints executors or administrators.
- Court-issued documents grant authority to collect estate assets; filing alone does not.
- Qualifying estates with $50,000 or less in personal property can use voluntary administration.
- WebSurrogate provides free case lookup; NYSCEF accepts electronic court filings.
- Elayne uses up to 10 years of tax transcripts and credit reports to build estate asset inventories.


## What NY Surrogate's Court Is


NY Surrogate's Court handles estates after a death, including validating wills and appointing someone to manage an estate. Each New York county has one. The court also handles certain related matters involving people who cannot manage their own affairs.


The Surrogate's Court Procedure Act (SCPA) sets the rules for its proceedings. Unlike courts that hear general civil disputes or criminal cases, Surrogate's Court is usually where an executor or administrator obtains legal authority to act on behalf of someone who died.


{{blog-cta-financial}}


## How NY Surrogate's Court Is Organized by County


Families generally file in the county where the person who died had their permanent home, legally called their domicile. Each county’s Surrogate’s Court has its own judge, clerk’s office, and administrative departments.


Court names may differ from city or borough names. Brooklyn’s Surrogate’s Court is in Kings County, Manhattan’s is in New York County, and Rochester’s is in Monroe County. Queens, Suffolk, and Nassau share their names with their respective county courts.


The county’s Surrogate’s Court website provides local filing procedures and department contacts.


## The Three Main Types of Proceedings


- Probate applies when there is a will. The court reviews its validity and appoints an executor.
- Administration applies when there is no will. Under SCPA Article 10, the court appoints an administrator; intestate succession rules determine inheritance.
- Voluntary administration, under SCPA Article 13, covers qualifying estates with $50,000 or less in personal property, with or without a will.


## Who Has Authority to Act: Executors, Administrators, and Voluntary Administrators


Being named in a will does not authorize collection of estate assets. Banks and agencies generally require proof of court appointment.


- [Letters Testamentary](https://www.elayne.com/resources/how-to-get-letters-testamentary-new-york) authorize the executor after the will is admitted to probate.
- [Letters of Administration](https://www.elayne.com/resources/how-to-get-letters-of-administration) authorize an administrator when there is no will. If no executor can serve under a will, the court appoints an administrator with the will annexed.
- A small-estate affidavit requests voluntary administration; court-issued certificates authorize collection of listed assets.


Filing alone grants no authority. The court must issue the appropriate document.


## NY Surrogate's Court Filing Fees


NY Surrogate's Court filing fees follow SCPA Section 2402’s statewide filing fee schedule. Fixed petition fees under SCPA 2402(8) apply to specified petitions separately from the variable schedule shown below.


For proceedings subject to the variable schedule:


Gross estate value Filing fee


Under $10,000 $45


$10,000 to under $20,000 $75


$20,000 to under $50,000 $215


$50,000 to under $100,000 $280


$100,000 to under $250,000 $420


$250,000 to under $500,000 $625


$500,000 and over $1,250


Filing costs depend on the proceeding and estate value. The court’s[official fee schedule](https://www.nycourts.gov/media/871) lists fixed petition fees; separate applications can carry further charges.


- Example estate value under the variable schedule: $100,000.
- Applicable band: $100,000 to under $250,000.
- Filing fee: $420.


## NY Surrogate's Court Forms


NY Surrogate's Court forms are available through the Unified Court System and county court websites. The main filing depends on the proceeding:


- Probate: a probate petition.
- Administration: a petition for administration.
- Voluntary administration: a voluntary administration affidavit.


For self-represented small-estate filers, the court's[DIY small estate program](https://www.nycourts.gov/help/diy-forms/small-estate-affidavit-program) helps prepare the affidavit.


County websites may provide local forms and checklists alongside statewide documents. The Surrogate's Court clerk's office can confirm which forms and supporting papers a particular proceeding requires, part of the broader[executor of estate paperwork](https://www.elayne.com/resources/executor-of-estate-paperwork) a filer may need to gather.


## How to Look Up a Surrogate's Court Case


[WebSurrogate's free statewide search](https://websurrogates.nycourts.gov/) provides NY Surrogate's Court case lookup for estate proceedings and other filings across counties. Key points to note:


- Name Search uses a party name; date of death can narrow results.
- File Search uses the court file number.
- Old Index Search retrieves available historical records.
- Will Search locates records of wills filed for safekeeping.


Guardianship proceedings and court-designated confidential files appear as “NOT PUBLIC,” with only basic file information visible. Details and documents are unavailable, as explained in the WebSurrogate public access guide.

## How Elayne Supports Families Working With NY Surrogate's Court


[Elayne](https://www.elayne.com/company) is an online service that supports families settling an estate after a death. It works through the estate one step at a time. Every family starts free, and Elayne offers 3 tiers that build on each other:


### Estate Setup


Estate Setup is for families who do not yet have legal authority (Letters Testamentary, Letters of Administration, or a voluntary administration certificate). It includes:


- An Estate Expert call, with slots opening within 24 hours, covering what comes next and which route may fit.
- Guided, step-by-step preparation of the court forms used to request legal authority, which the family then files.
- A check of whether a small estate process, such as voluntary administration, may apply.
- An introduction to a vetted attorney in the family's state, when one is requested.
- Receipt tracking for estate costs, including the Estate Setup fee.
- The deceased notification sent to the credit bureaus, so no new credit can be opened in the person's name.
- An encrypted document vault, with unlimited invites for family members and professionals.


### Asset Search


Elayne Asset Search (IRS-authorized · Equifax-powered) is for families who have legal authority or are about to. Portions of the search can begin before the court issues papers, and legal authority opens the full search.


Elayne holds IRS authorization to request the person's IRS tax transcripts. An IRS tax transcript is not a tax return. It shows what banks, insurers, workplaces, and retirement account custodians reported to the IRS about the person over 10 years.


The search also includes the person's Equifax credit report, the life insurance locators, the pension registry, the national unclaimed property database, and property and vehicle records. Each finding is added to an estate inventory that names its source, with debts listed alongside assets.


### Estate Settlement


Estate Settlement is for families who have legal authority and are handling the estate's money. It includes obtaining the estate's tax ID (EIN), help opening the estate bank account, and monitoring of deposits and payments. Elayne works through what each bank or company needs to release an account, pre-fills transfer forms, tracks what the estate owes the executor, and prepares the final accounting with receipts attached.

## FAQ


### Can you use WebSurrogate for a NY Surrogate's Court case lookup if you live in California or Texas?


Yes, WebSurrogate’s online public search is available from outside New York. Your location does not change which county holds the estate file; searches generally focus on the county where the person who died had their permanent home.


### How do you find surrogate court records when WebSurrogate returns no results?


Trying alternate name spellings, a court file number, or Old Index Search can help locate a record. If no match appears, the county Surrogate’s Court clerk can confirm whether a file exists and how available records can be requested. A missing search result does not prove that no estate proceeding has been filed.


### Which county's Surrogate's Court handles an estate in New York?


Families generally file in the county where the person who died had their permanent home, legally called their domicile. Each county's Surrogate's Court has its own judge, clerk's office, and administrative departments. The county court's website provides local filing procedures and department contacts.


### Which Surrogate's Court covers Brooklyn, Manhattan, and Rochester?


Brooklyn's Surrogate's Court is in Kings County, Manhattan's is in New York County, and Rochester's is in Monroe County. Queens, Suffolk, and Nassau share their names with their respective county courts. Court names can differ from city or borough names.


### What is the difference between Letters Testamentary and Letters of Administration?


Letters Testamentary authorize the executor after the will is admitted to probate. Letters of Administration authorize an administrator when there is no will. If no executor can serve under a will, the court appoints an administrator with the will annexed.
